summary: Insulin isophane (NPH; human isophane insulin) is an intermediate-acting human insulin indicated to improve glycaemic control in adults and children with diabetes mellitus. It is a cloudy, white SUSPENSION that must be gently resuspended (rolled/inverted) before each use and is given by subcutaneous injection only - it must NEVER be given intravenously or used in an insulin pump. Dosing is fully individualised to metabolic needs, blood glucose monitoring and glycaemic goals, and it is often combined with a meal-time insulin. Hypoglycaemia is the most common and potentially life-threatening adverse reaction; hypokalaemia may also occur.
indications: To improve glycaemic control in adults with diabetes mellitus
To improve glycaemic control in paediatric patients with diabetes mellitus

dosage.r: Subcutaneous injection (abdominal wall, thigh, upper arm or buttock)
dosage.d: Individualised - no fixed dose; titrate to metabolic needs and glucose goals
dosage.t: As prescribed (e.g. once or twice daily basal); increase glucose monitoring with regimen changes
dosage.n: May be used with a prandial insulin; rotate injection sites within a region

dosage.d: Individualised to metabolic needs and glucose goals

admin: Subcutaneous use ONLY - do NOT give intravenously and do NOT use in an insulin infusion pump
It is a suspension - inspect before use; gently roll/resuspend so it is uniformly cloudy; do not use if particulate matter remains or it does not mix evenly
Inject into the subcutaneous tissue of the abdominal wall, thigh, upper arm or buttock and rotate sites within the region to reduce lipodystrophy and localised cutaneous amyloidosis
Do not inject into areas of lipodystrophy or cutaneous amyloidosis
If mixed with regular human insulin or rapid-acting insulin, draw the clear (regular/rapid) insulin into the syringe FIRST, then inject immediately after mixing
Never share a pen, needle or syringe between patients even if the needle is changed (blood-borne pathogen risk)
Always check the insulin label before each injection to avoid mix-ups; increase glucose monitoring when changing the regimen
moa: Insulin isophane lowers blood glucose by stimulating peripheral glucose uptake into skeletal muscle and fat and by inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Insulin also inhibits lipolysis and proteolysis and enhances protein synthesis. As an isophane (NPH) suspension it is absorbed slowly from the subcutaneous depot, giving an intermediate duration of action.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to insulin isophane or any of its excipients
relative: Hypoglycaemia unawareness or longstanding diabetes / autonomic neuropathy
Concurrent use of beta-blockers or other agents that blunt hypoglycaemia warning signs
Concomitant thiazolidinedione (PPAR-gamma agonist) use - fluid retention/heart failure risk
monitor: Blood glucose, especially with any change in regimen, activity, diet or illness
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hypokalaemia
Signs of heart failure if used with a thiazolidinedione
Injection sites for lipodystrophy or cutaneous amyloidosis

preg: Published data over decades have not established an association between human insulin use in pregnancy and major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal/fetal outcomes. Poorly controlled diabetes itself increases maternal and fetal risk, so glycaemic control should be maintained; insulin requirements often change during pregnancy and require close monitoring and dose adjustment.
lact: Published literature suggests exogenous human insulin, including isophane insulin, is transferred into human milk, but no adverse reactions in breastfed infants have been reported and there are no data on effects on milk production. Consider the benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother's clinical need and any potential effect on the infant.
renal: The effect of renal impairment on pharmacokinetics has not been formally studied. Patients with renal impairment are at increased risk of hypoglycaemia and may need more frequent dose adjustment and more frequent blood glucose monitoring.
hepatic: The effect of hepatic impairment on pharmacokinetics has not been formally studied. Patients with hepatic impairment are at increased risk of hypoglycaemia and may need more frequent dose adjustment and more frequent blood glucose monitoring.

major: Drugs increasing hypoglycaemia risk: other antidiabetic agents, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, disopyramide, fibrates, fluoxetine, MAO inhibitors, pentoxifylline, pramlintide, salicylates, octreotide, sulfonamide antibiotics - may need dose reduction and increased monitoring
Thiazolidinediones (PPAR-gamma agonists) - dose-related fluid retention that may cause or worsen heart failure when combined with insulin
moderate: Drugs reducing glucose-lowering effect: atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine), corticosteroids, danazol, diuretics, oestrogens, glucagon, isoniazid, niacin, oral contraceptives, phenothiazines, progestogens, protease inhibitors, somatropin, sympathomimetics (albuterol, epinephrine, terbutaline), thyroid hormones - may need dose increase and monitoring
Pentamidine - may cause hypoglycaemia sometimes followed by hyperglycaemia
minor: Beta-blockers, clonidine, guanethidine, reserpine - may blunt or mask the warning signs and symptoms of hypoglycaemia
interactions.food: Basal insulin; matching of dose to food intake and meal timing affects glucose; skipped or inadequate meals increase hypoglycaemia risk
interactions.alcohol: Alcohol may either increase or decrease the blood-glucose-lowering effect (with beta-blockers, clonidine and lithium salts in the same category); use with caution and monitor glucose
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor blood glucose and HbA1c; check serum potassium in patients at risk of hypokalaemia

serious: Severe hypoglycaemia - can cause seizures, may be life-threatening or fatal
Hypokalaemia - may cause respiratory paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia and death if untreated
Fluid retention and heart failure when combined with a thiazolidinedione
rare: Localised cutaneous amyloidosis at injection sites
emergency: Severe hypoglycaemia with coma, seizure or neurological impairment - treat with a glucagon product or intravenous glucose
Anaphylaxis - discontinue and treat per standard of care

monitoring: Self-monitoring of blood glucose, with increased frequency when starting therapy or changing the regimen, dose, activity or diet
HbA1c periodically to assess overall glycaemic control
Serum potassium in patients at risk of hypokalaemia
Signs and symptoms of hypoglycaemia (and hypoglycaemia unawareness)
Signs of heart failure if used with a thiazolidinedione
Injection sites for lipodystrophy / cutaneous amyloidosis
counsel: This insulin is a cloudy suspension - gently roll or invert the vial or pen to mix it evenly before each dose; do not shake vigorously and do not use if clumps remain
Inject under the skin only - never inject it into a vein, and never use it in an insulin pump
Rotate your injection sites within the same area to avoid lumps or pitting of the skin
Learn to recognise and treat low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion); carry a fast-acting sugar source
Low blood sugar can impair your concentration and reaction time - use caution when driving or operating machinery, especially if you have frequent or unaware lows
Always check the insulin label before each injection to avoid mixing up insulin types
Never share your pen, needle or syringe with anyone else, even with a new needle
Tell your doctor about illness, changes in diet, activity, or other medicines as your insulin dose may need adjustment
pk: Intermediate-acting - slower onset than regular human insulin (about 1-2 hours)
Median maximum glucose-lowering effect around 6.5 hours (range 2.8-13 h); peak serum insulin about 4 hours after subcutaneous dosing
Absorption-rate limited; mean apparent half-life about 4.4 hours (range 1-84 h) - a true half-life cannot be accurately estimated
Intermediate duration of action (longer than regular insulin); time course varies between and within individuals

Protect from heat and light; do not freeze or use if frozen. Unopened: refrigerate (2-8 C) until expiry. Vial: room temperature (up to 30 C) for 31 days in-use/not-in-use; KwikPen: room temperature up to 14 days (do not refrigerate in use)
pearls: Hypoglycaemia is the most common and the most serious adverse effect - it can be life-threatening and symptoms vary between and within patients over time
It is a cloudy SUSPENSION: always resuspend (roll/invert) before use - inadequate mixing causes inconsistent dosing
NPH/isophane must NEVER be given intravenously and must NOT be used in an insulin infusion pump
Intermediate-acting: slower onset (~1-2 h) with a peak around the mid-point and an intermediate duration; the peak is when hypoglycaemia risk is highest
When mixing with regular or rapid insulin, draw the clear insulin first then inject immediately
Beta-blockers and other antiadrenergic drugs can mask the warning signs of hypoglycaemia
All insulins shift potassium intracellularly - watch for hypokalaemia, especially with overdose or other potassium-lowering drugs
missed: If a dose is missed, do not double the next dose. Check blood glucose and follow the prescriber's sick-day/missed-dose instructions; an unexpected change in insulin dosing or meal timing can cause hyperglycaemia (if under-dosed) or hypoglycaemia. Resume the usual regimen and increase glucose monitoring after any disruption.
overdose: Excess insulin causes hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. Mild hypoglycaemia is treated with oral glucose and adjustment of dose, meals or activity. More severe episodes with coma, seizure or neurological impairment are treated with a glucagon product or concentrated intravenous glucose. Hypoglycaemia may recur after apparent recovery, so sustained carbohydrate intake and observation are needed; correct hypokalaemia appropriately.
